title: ACID vs BASE
tagline: The two database philosophies: strict transactional guarantees vs soft, available, eventually-consistent ones.

paragraphs: ACID is the set of guarantees classic relational databases give around a **transaction** — a group of operations treated as one indivisible unit. It's what lets you move money between two accounts without ever losing or duplicating it.

items.detail: All operations in a transaction succeed, or none do. A transfer that debits A but crashes before crediting B is rolled back entirely — no half-states.
A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting all rules/constraints (foreign keys, checks). Note: this is a *different* 'consistency' than CAP's.

Concurrent transactions don't step on each other; the result is as if they ran one at a time. Isolation levels (read committed, repeatable read, serializable) tune how strict this is vs how much concurrency you allow.
Once committed, data survives crashes and power loss — it's persisted (e.g., via a write-ahead log).

blocks.text: The 'C' in ACID (valid states per constraints) is NOT the 'C' in CAP (every read sees the latest write). Interviewers love this distinction — don't conflate them.

paragraphs: Many NoSQL systems deliberately relax ACID to scale horizontally and stay highly available. Their philosophy is summarised as **BASE**, a tongue-in-cheek opposite of ACID (acid vs base, chemistry pun).

items.detail: The system guarantees availability — it responds to every request, even if some responses are stale or degraded.
State may change over time even without new input, as replicas sync in the background; there's no single instant of 'the' truth.
Given no new writes, all replicas converge to the same value eventually. Readers may briefly see old data.

blocks.text: BASE is essentially the AP corner of CAP applied as a design philosophy: prefer availability and partition tolerance, accept eventual consistency. It trades strict guarantees for massive scale and uptime.

rows: Money, orders, inventory, anything needing correctness
Coordination → latency, harder to scale writes
Complexity pushed to the app (conflict handling)

blocks.title: The mature answer: use both
blocks.text: Real systems are polyglot. Use an ACID/SQL store for the parts that demand correctness (payments, orders), and a BASE/NoSQL store for the parts that demand scale and can tolerate staleness (activity feeds, view counts, sessions). Stating this 'right tool per data type' reasoning is the senior move — far better than 'NoSQL is more scalable so use it everywhere'.

cheatsheet: ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — strong transactional guarantees (classic SQL).
BASE = Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency — relaxed guarantees for scale/availability (many NoSQL).
ACID's 'C' (valid states/constraints) ≠ CAP's 'C' (latest read). Don't conflate them.
ACID for correctness (money/orders/inventory); BASE for scale + staleness-tolerant data (feeds/counts).
Mature systems are polyglot — pick the store per data type, not one for everything.

questions.prompt: Explain atomicity and isolation using a bank transfer, and what breaks without each.
questions.hint: One is about partial failure; the other about concurrent transfers.
answer: Atomicity: transferring $100 from A to B is debit-A + credit-B as one unit. Without atomicity, a crash after the debit but before the credit destroys $100 — money vanishes. Atomicity guarantees both happen or neither does (rollback on failure).

Isolation: if two transfers touch account A at the same time, isolation makes them behave as if run sequentially, so they don't read/overwrite each other's intermediate state. Without it you get race conditions like lost updates — e.g., two withdrawals both reading the same starting balance and overdrawing the account.
keyPoints: Atomicity: all-or-nothing, prevents money vanishing on partial failure
Isolation: concurrent txns don't interfere, prevents lost-update races
Both protect correctness of the transfer
followUps: What isolation level would you need to prevent the lost-update, and what's its cost?

questions.prompt: An e-commerce site needs to store orders, payments, product catalog, and a 'recently viewed' list. Which want ACID and which are fine with BASE?
questions.hint: Which data, if briefly stale or partially written, causes real harm?
answer: Orders and payments need **ACID**: a payment must be atomic and durable, and you can't have an order half-created or charged twice. Inventory decrement also wants strong guarantees to avoid overselling. Put these in a transactional SQL store.

Product catalog and 'recently viewed' are fine with **BASE**: a catalog can be eventually consistent (a price/description propagating over seconds is acceptable, and it's read-heavy — great for caching/replication), and 'recently viewed' is per-user, non-critical, and tolerant of staleness or even occasional loss. Splitting storage this way gives correctness where it matters and scale where it doesn't.
followUps: How would you keep inventory strongly consistent while the catalog stays eventually consistent?
